https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: Learn what yesterday’s big changes mean for the non-Space Marines factions.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
The latest Warhammer 40,000 balance update dropped yesterday, making Space Marines of different kinds faster, tougher, and more deadly. But what do those changes mean for the other armies of the 41st Millennium?

An increase in AP on boltguns and chainswords is a new challenge to overcome for units universally. It will encourage some factions to pivot to defensively focused detachments, or units with an invulnerable save that is the same or better than their default save characteristic, to minimise this change on your army. This is also dependent on what role you want a unit to play in your army. 

For example, you are playing Tyranids and you have deployed Termagants to act as a screening* unit to protect your Excocrine from being charged by some Deep Striking Chaos Space Marine Terminators. Regardless of your opponent’s shooting, the Terminators are unable to charge your more important Exocrine due to the increased distance you created using your Termagants. Boltguns being more powerful doesn’t change the fact that your Termagants have fulfilled their purpose, and if your opponent has included more boltguns instead of a lascannon, a plasma gun, or a meltagun, then their efficacy against your more valuable Exocrine will be reduced.

There will also typically be fewer Space Marines on the battlefield to shoot or charge, likely meaning your opponent will be looking to maximise their points with the most effective units available to them, so boltguns and chainswords may be the least of your worries.

This also means that although Space Marines are tougher to kill now, fewer Space Marines on the battlefield means your own units also have fewer things to kill. In the above example, the Exocrine, although wounding them on a 3+ now, has fewer to kill, and offers more value through each one it does destroy. 

As Space Marine variants make up the majority of armies within Warhammer 40,000, it’s generally wise to construct your army assuming you will be battling them at some point. Many of the units that were good at killing Space Marines are still good at it. Brôkhyr Thunderkyn, Doomsday Arks, Howling Banshees, Riptides, and Knight Despoilers will continue to cause problems for the Adeptus Astartes.

So having broken down what the impacts are, what are the upsides to this change for you?

As we’ve said, there are going to be fewer Space Marine bodies actually on the battlefield, which will change how they approach the game. They won’t be able to trade** for objectives as well as many non-Space Marine armies, and they will find it more challenging to hold down objectives and safely achieve secondary objectives. More horde-focussed armies such as Astra Militarum, Drukhari, and Genestealer Cults will be better equipped to trade bodies into the brutal meat grinder for that sweet victory.

The increase in strength to boltguns and chainswords has mixed degrees of value against your armies. For the average Human, Aeldari, Leman Russ, or Goliath Rock Grinder, this change means nothing, as it’s not enough to improve their odds to wound against these types of targets. 

This all comes with new strategies, new army compositions, new challenges, and new triumphs to achieve, all of which requires some trial and error to find the right way to approach and overcome. So don’t be disheartened if you don’t find your army running rampant across the fields of Chogoris or wastes of Baal immediately – even Abaddon took 13 tries to crack Cadia, remember?

Download the latest balance update now so you can be ready for whatever the Space Marines try and throw at you.

* A screening unit is one that is cheap in points and often used to deny your opponent movement. This might be through standing in the way and physically blocking opposing models, by denying areas of the board for units to arrive from strategic reserves, or to make it harder for your opponent to charge into another target.
** Trading means units that are typically more effective for their points cost at holding and challenging for objectives than their opponents, generally by destroying units more expensive in points than themselves.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: Warhammer 40,000 – Balance Update: Emboldened Astartes
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: Heretics and Loyalists alike are receiving a suite of updates in time for the release of Codex: Space Marines.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
Another big update has arrived for Warhammer 40,000 and sees many of your favourite ceramite-clad warriors getting stronger, tougher, more deadly, or some combination of all three!

With the impending release of Codex: Space Marines, Astartes of every ilk will see changes to some of their characteristics, which will be some combination of their Move, their Toughness, or some of their weapon options.

So which factions are affected? The list includes:

  • Black Templars

  • Blood Angels

  • Chaos Space Marines

  • Dark Angels

  • Death Guard

  • Deathwatch

  • Emperor’s Children

  • Grey Knights

  • Space Wolves

  • Thousand Sons

  • World Eaters

  • Imperial Agents

Movement

Starting off with movement changes, Phobos armoured Space Marines will be increasing their Move characteristic to a whopping 8” while staying at Toughness 4. This better reflects the lighter and more manoeuvreable armour these warriors are equipped with and allows them to play a different role within your armies – namely, fast moving units, ideally suited to harrying other weaker units (especially those with Toughness 4 or lower and a single Wound), blocking movement,* and scoring objectives requiring positioning or actions. No longer will you be just short of scoring that crucial objective. However, these units will see a points increase as a result of getting faster.

Toughness

The most widespread change is Toughness – most Space Marines will now have an extra point of Toughness. This covers Tacticus armour, Terminator armour, and many Chaos units.** It won’t include units in Gravis armour, the previously mentioned Phobos squads, or the Death Guard.

So what does this mean? All units that are increasing in Toughness can also expect an increase to their points. Your armies will likely see a dramatic change, most certainly fielding fewer units, but you can expect those units to be more survivable against small arms fire. It may also change how your army plays, by encouraging different detachment combinations and Force Dispositions. 

Weapons

As previously mentioned, some weapon options see changes. Namely the workhorses for each Space Marine faction – boltguns (of various kinds) and chainswords (as well as other similar close quarters weapons). These generally gain a point of Strength, going to 5, and in some cases earn a point of AP. 

The Sons of Mortarion

This might be most impactful for the Death Guard, their boltguns and plague knives both getting the S5 and AP-1 treatment. Plus, with their Nurgle’s Gift army rule, their odds of wounding and being wounded by other Astartes factions doesn’t change, but the chance of inflicting damage increases due to that extra AP. Knowing the other factions will see points increases and fewer models in their armies, every point of damage goes further than ever. And with the Death Guard not increasing in Toughness, they aren’t seeing the associated point increases.

Does all this mean that Nurgle is in ascendancy? Only time will tell.

Finally, the Adeptus Custodes will see some small changes to their bolt weaponry to give you a taste for the gloriously golden updates that will be unleashed with their impending new Codex.

What happens if you don’t play some variation of boltgun-wielding giant? Check in tomorrow where we will discuss this further. In the meantime, download the new balance update now.

Warhammer 40,000 September Update

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: How To Keep Your Custodians Standing Sentinel
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: The forces of the Adeptus Custodes are tough but even they have their limits against the threats of the 41st Millennium.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
The Adeptus Custodes are now tough – very tough – with a typical Toughness of 7 or higher*. This means that many weapons designed to tackle infantry aren't going to make the same impact but, as always, there are exceptions to the rule. Here’s what budding Shield-Captains need to keep an eye on.

There are a number of weapon abilities to watch for: Anti-X, Devastating Wounds, Lance, Lethal Hits, and Melta. Each of these are threatening for different reasons, and many armies have numerous ways of accessing them.

Anti-X, commonly Anti-Infantry, cheats the Toughness of your Custodian Guard by just ignoring it. Armies such as the Adeptus Mechanicus and Drukhari have a selection of units with this weapon ability by default, and with a key stratagem at the right time, the correct leader attached to that unit, or a particular aura, the efficiency of units such as Hastarii Exterminators, Kataphron Breachers, Scourges with Heavy Weapons or Wracks** can become problematic for your proud defenders of the Golden Throne.

Lance is another weapon ability that, to a lesser extent, upsets your incredible Toughness. Armies like Blood Angels have many ways to challenge for the number one gold armour spot, turning an otherwise meagre chance to wound into a more significant probability. Pay particular attention to Sanguinary Guard, their encarmine spears having Lance by default, especially when combined with The Angelic Host detachment rule which increases their efficiency to hit and wound, may punish you for trying to prove your superiority. 

Similarly, an honourable mention should be given to the forces of the Black Templars, their Templar Vows offering them the fitting Accept any Challenge, no Matter the Odds ability, which provides an equally impactful improvement to the wound roll that Lance offers just without the need to even charge.

Lethal Hits ignores the wound process in its entirety, which affects all armies equally, but when you’ve got the most elite fighting force in the galaxy, this can prove worrisome. Both Death Guard and Chaos Space Marines should be approached with caution – almost every Death Guard unit has a weapon with Lethal Hits, none more potent than Deathshroud Terminators (who also sport Anti-Infantry 4+ plaguespurt gauntlets). Additionally, most Chaos Space Marines units can get Lethal Hits through Dark Pacts, and Chosen (especially being led by Huron Blackheart and the Masters of the Maelstrom) have a huge number of attacks with sufficient AP to ensure your Custodians will need to rely on their invulnerable save.

CHAOS SPACE MARINES ARMY RULE

DARK PACTS

If your Army Faction is HERETIC ASTARTES, each time a unit with this ability is selected to shoot or fight, it can make a Dark Pact. If it does, it must first take a Leadership test before any effects of that Dark Pact are resolved; if that test is failed, that unit suffers D3 mortal wounds. Then, select one of the following abilities for that unit's weapons to gain until the end of the phase:

  • [LETHAL HITS]

  • [SUSTAINED HITS 1]

Melta is dangerous in an entirely different way. It won’t make your Toughness count for less, but it will make those high Wounds models suffer for every failed invulnerable saving throw, due to the bonus damage at half range. Space Marine Eradicators and Aeldari Fire Dragons are examples that carry potent weapons with the Melta weapon ability. Adepta Sororitas Retributors can also bring the pain by using Miracle dice from their Acts of Faith army rule to maximise the damage they push through.

Lastly, Devastating Wounds is an unreliable, but perhaps the most threatening, option against an army composed of few models. Every critical wound rolled is one you can’t take a save against, relying instead on your Feel No Pain 5+ versus mortal wounds, meaning that your statuesque demi-gods may rapidly find themselves in trouble. Some potent deliverers of this are World Eaters and Chaos Daemons. 

World Eaters require a bit of luck to be blessed with Decapitating Strikes, from the Blessings of Khorne, but it is possible for their entire army to have Devastating Wounds on their melee attacks against Infantry units, making units like Eightbound or large units of Khorne Berzerkers capable of pulling down unfortunate Custodians should they manage to roll a few lucky 6s. 

Chaos Daemons are also one to be wary of, such as Skulltaker leading a band of merry Bloodletters. He provides Devastating Wounds to their melee attacks, which can be supplemented by other units, such as a Rendmaster’s Blood Throne ability, to improve their S, AP and D characteristics by 1 for each assisting Rendmaster, before he himself strikes.

WORLD EATERS ARMY RULE

BLESSINGS OF KHORNE

If your Army Faction is WORLD EATERS, at the start of the battle round, you can make a Blessings of Khorne roll. To do so, roll eight D6. You can then use those dice to activate up to two Blessings of Khorne (see right). Each Blessing of Khorne specifies the dice results it requires (where a number is specified, a double or triple of that value or higher is required). You can only activate each Blessing of Khorne once per battle round. Any unused dice from the Blessings of Khorne roll are then discarded. Once activated, each Blessing of Khorne applies to all units from your army with this ability until the end of the battle round.

DECAPITATING STRIKES

Each time a model in this unit makes a melee attack that targets an INFANTRY unit, that attack has the [DEVASTATING WOUNDS] ability.

Of course, there should also be attention given to units with large numbers of attacks at high damage. Imperial and Chaos Knights have many units that can destroy a model in a single strike, Chaos Daemons have Skarbrand offering skulls at an alarming rate, and Orks have the Prophet of the Waaagh! himself – Ghazghkull Thraka – to name just a few who will punish an Adeptus Custodes force should you fail to make an adequate number of save rolls. So just don’t fail your save rolls. Easy, right?***

With key preparation and awareness your Adeptus Custodes will be a force to be reckoned with and many of these challenges will be overcome by destroying your foe before they become a problem or utilising your defensive options to limit the punishment they attempt to inflict.

The new Codex: Adeptus Custodes is available to pre-order from Saturday. Make sure you come back later in the week when we’ll be taking a look at some of our favourite ways to mix-and-match the detachments from the book.

* Excluding the forces of the Anathema Psykana.
** Especially if combined with the Distillers of Fear stratagem in the Covenite Coterie detachment, due to how Devastating Wounds combines with Anti-Infantry.
*** We can’t guarantee that the dice coming out alongside the Codex are blessed by the Emperor, but they can’t hurt.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: Your first look at 13 new Adeptus Custodes detachments
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: New rules revealed from the forthcoming Codex: Adeptus Custodes.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
Take a look at the new Warhammer 40,000 detachments for the Adeptus Custodes. When combined with their souped-up datasheets and deadly martial ka’tah abilities, they make for an intimidating force.

Where selecting Orks detachments is a chaotic free-for-all and choosing Space Marines detachments is more regimented and orderly, the Adeptus Custodes sit somewhere between the two. Only one group of their detachments has a Unique keyword, while the rest can be chosen freely to boost units like Dreadnoughts, Terminators, or Sisters of Silence. 

Six of the 13 detachments available in the Codex have the Unique: Shield Host tag, five of which are themed after one of the main Shield Hosts laid out in the lore section.* The Aquilan Shield, for instance, plays a more defensive game, focused on occupying objectives and whittling down the enemy as they’re forced to come to you, while the aggressive Dread Host charges forwards as fast as possible to brutalise their foes in close combat.

One thing you’ll notice – probably because we mentioned it on Friday – is that the Shield Host detachments each have a favoured ka’tah in addition to their detachment rule. These give additional effects when the corresponding ka’tah is activated, so if you activate Dacatarai for your units while using the Dread Host detachment, those units will re-roll 1s to hit against non-Monster/Vehicle units and reduce the pile-in and consolidation moves for engaged enemies by 2” – giving them a serious advantage over larger enemy units that now can’t get all of their warriors into engagement range.

Don’t worry about scuppering your tactical options, though, as having a favoured ka’tah doesn’t prevent you from using any others. It’s just a bonus.

Likewise, the Aquilan Shield gets bonus range on their guns when they use the Salvus ka’tah, and this helps them engage even more foes as they come crashing against your shield wall. This detachment has plenty of tools to soften up the enemy before the melee begins, like extra Strength from the Tip of the Talon stratagem, and can even gun them down as they foolishly fall back from a hopelessly one-sided scrap with Rapid Reactions.

TIP OF THE TALON (1CP)

AQUILAN SHIELD STRATAGEM

Fighting at the forefront of the battle, these Custodians hit their victims with perfectly timed volleys the instant before they tear into their ranks. 

WHEN: Your Shooting phase, when a friendly ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit is selected to shoot.

TARGET: That ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit. 

EFFECT: Your unit’s ranged attacks that target an enemy unit within 9" of your unit have +1 S.

RAPID REACTIONS (1CP)

AQUILAN SHIELD STRATAGEM

Forcing their outmatched enemies to fall back, Custodians level their guardian spears and cut down fleeing opponents with volleys of bolter fire.

WHEN: Your opponent’s Movement phase, when an enemy unit ends a fall-back move.

TARGET: One friendly ADEPTUS CUSTODES INFANTRY unit that was engaged with that enemy unit at the start of the phase. 

EFFECT: Your unit shoots using normal shooting, but while doing so your unit can only target that enemy unit.

If wholesale destruction is more your speed, Dread Host gets you there quickly with a dose of Preternatural Rapidity allowing charges after an advance move – a favourite of assault-focused armies. 

This detachment’s enhancements boost a Shield-Captain or Blade Champion, making them an Auric Exemplar and giving them Cleave 1 or calling out their Flawless Bladework and rewarding them with Sustained Hits 1.  We’re especially fond of putting the latter on a Blade Champion’s eight Precision Victus attacks – it’s a great way to cut the head off the snake before it even knows you’re swinging.

PRETERNATURAL RAPIDITY (1CP)

DREAD HOST STRATAGEM

The warriors of the Adeptus Custodes are relentless in their pursuit of the Throneworld’s foes.

WHEN: Your Movement phase, when a friendly ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit ends an advance move.

TARGET: That ADEPTUS CUSTODES unit. 

EFFECT: That advance move does not prevent your unit from being eligible to declare a charge.

ENHANCEMENTS

FLAWLESS BLADEWORK

This Custodian’s skills in close-quarters combat are awe-inspiring to behold.

ADEPTUS CUSTODES model only. This model’s melee attacks have [SUSTAINED HITS 1].

You might have spotted some detachment names during the Big Autumn Preview stream, so we won’t beat around the bush – here’s what they are, and what they do.

  • Guardians of the Throne – A big 3DP detachment giving balanced bonuses to most units.

  • Aquilan Shield & Dread Host – See above! (Unique: Shield Host)

  • Emissaries Imperatus – Prioritise the mission, fight first, and ignore modifiers to hit and wound. (Unique: Shield Host)

  • Emperor’s Chosen – Make your units more flexible and reliable, and ready a ka’tah mid-round too. (Unique: Shield Host)

  • Shadowkeepers – Brawl in close combat and overwhelm your enemy. (Unique: Shield Host)

  • Solar Watch – Move even quicker than usual, and flow into and out of engagement like water. (Unique: Shield Host)

  • Auric Champions – Character models single out prey and show why they’re your army’s champions.

  • Honoured Companions – Custodian Guard, Sentinel Guard and Wardens contest vital objectives.

  • Lions of the Emperor – Unleash your Terminators. Deep Strike, charge, cause carnage, and split your Terminator units mid-battle.

  • Might of the Moritoi – The galaxy’s best Dreadnoughts get escalating combat bonuses as they take damage.

  • Grav-assault Force – Grav-tanks support your forces and outflank opponents to sneakily secure objectives.

  • Null Maiden Vigil – The Sisters of Silence! Take one as your WARLORD with BATTLELINE Prosecutor squads.

That’s loads of versatility that can really be focused into some key units, thanks to the faction’s compact unit count. Pick your favourite Shield Host, then layer other detachments on top of the models you like the most for some real champion-level power.

The Adeptus Custodes are pretty powerful, but even they have things to fear in the 41st Millennium. Join us tomorrow as we take a look at some of the things even the Ten Thousand need to be wary of.

* Aquilan Shield, Dread Host, Emissaries Imperatus, Shadowkeepers, and Solar Watch.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: Warriors of Chaos armies fresh from the Studio
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: The team behind Warhammer: The Old World pledge fealty to the Dark Gods.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
With the release of spectacular new miniatures for the Warriors of Chaos, a wave of corruption has swept through the Warhammer Studio. We’ve seen frenzied activity from several members of the team, all eager to get their new models onto the battlefield, so we just had to show them off.

Danny

I started this project by painting two large units, one of Marauders and one of Chaos Warriors, my plan being to have a solid core of infantry completed before moving on to more elite units, characters and monsters. Making full use of the options available to them, my Marauders are armed with hand weapons, flails and shields, and this is reflected by combining models armed with hand weapons and shields with flail-armed models in a single unit. Mixing them in this way shows my opponents how the unit is equipped, and really suits their barbarous and unruly nature.

The Skin Wolves also deserve special mention here – I’ve been a fan of the Wolves of the Sea Army of Infamy since the beginning of its development and have played with it a lot. For me, the Skin Wolves are an iconic unit from that Army Composition list and I couldn’t resist getting some painted up.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Chaos Lord on Dragon was the (not so) miniature I enjoyed painting the most. It was nice to put into practice the skills honed on previous projects on such an awesome centrepiece miniature. I am really pleased with the final product and can’t wait to terrorise my regular opponents with my new beastie!

I’ve got a unit of Chaos Marauder Horsemen and a host of Chaos Knights on my hobby desk at the moment. Once they are finished, I plan to add some Dragon Ogres, Chariots, and a second Chaos Dragon, this time ridden by a Sorcerer Lord!

Quinn

The new Chaos Warriors were a real treat for me, as they both subtly hark back to the plastic Chaos Warriors from the nineties (my first ever Warhammer kit),* and let me finally try my hand at recreating the ‘Iron Wolves’, as featured in White Dwarf 290.

As an expansion for my all-marauder Wolves of the Sea Battle March army, most of my paint scheme was already established, but as the warriors are so heavily armoured I knew that using a metallic undercoat would pay dividends. Where on the Marauders I applied a Mechanicus Standard Grey zenithal spray and a Corax White drybrush over Rhinox Hide, for the Warriors I subbed in a Leadbelcher zenithal and Stormhost Silver drybrush. This gave me the same warm undertone in the recesses with a cool gradient over the top, just with a metallic finish. Over this, all I needed to complete the armour was a Coelia Greenshade wash, followed by Ironjawz Yellow on the trim and a final drybrush of Ironbreaker, meaning these models went from bare plastic to looking almost table-ready very quickly.

Following this first batch of five test models, I’ve got plenty more Warriors of Chaos underway, as they’ll form the core of a regiment of 17 Warriors joined by a battle standard bearer, with a champion-led block of Chaos Knights waiting in the wings. Building them all at once also allowed me to swap heads, shoulders and shields between the Warriors and Knights, which is a great way of maximising variety in the units and hint at the Knights’ higher status with careful selection of components.

Dave

I’ve always been a fan of the Chaos Warriors, their armour-clad forms looming over the brave heroes or noble knights of the enemy. With the release of Arcane Journal: The March of Chaos, I was very much drawn to the Hordes of Chaos Army of Infamy, and loved the idea of Warriors of Chaos and Beastmen Brayherds united in their disdain for the weak nations of the Old World who cower behind their city walls.

I personally prefer armies of untamed, undivided Chaos – the kind that wants to tear down civilisation and cover the land in darkness. It’s so classically and satisfyingly evil, and evokes the looming sense of constant doom synonymous with the World of Legend. With this in mind, I wanted to paint my warriors in colours that had a primal, bestial feel to them, as though they’d given themselves over to utter ruination. Whilst the classic dark iron armour is iconic, I wanted to try something different…

I used Runelord Brass for the majority of the armour, washed with Agrax Earthshade and then highlighted with Canoptek Alloy. I then painted the armour trim with Iron Warriors, and the furs and cloaks with Abaddon Black and Eshin Grey respectively, shading all of them with Nuln Oil and then drybrushing with lighter shades (which was an absolute breeze with how beautifully detailed the new models are). Overall this created a dramatic visual contrast between the warm, primal brass and cold, merciless steel, really capturing the contradictory nature of Chaos Undivided.

I sadly didn’t finish painting my Chaos Dragon in time to feature here, but the big, green monstrosity is going to be joining my army very soon, along with a hearty block of Gors and a Ghorgon for good measure.

Thanks, folks! If you want to take your first steps into the World of Legend grab the Warhammer: The Old World Core Set and decide whether to desecrate the land with the Warriors of Chaos or defend it with the Armies of Grand Cathay.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: Ride for ruin with our Rohan™ tactical advice
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: Top tactical tips from a Middle-earth™ Strategy Battle Game veteran.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
With the updated Riders of Rohan thundering across the battlefields of Middle-earth, we decided it was time to get some tactical tips for all Marshals of the Riddermark. Fortunately for us, Middle-earth Strategy Battle Game community veteran Kalman Steels answered our call for aid in a thorough assessment of the armies of Rohan.

Kalman: The Kingdom of Rohan really doesn’t need much of an introduction. A favourite for movie and book fans alike, it is also one of the most popular factions in the Middle-earth Strategy Battle Game. Famous for their glorious and devastating cavalry charges, Rohan are the faction to use if you want to ride out and meet your opponent for death and glory.* 

I’ll begin by looking at the strengths and weaknesses that come with a Rohan army, and then dig into how to make the most of them on the battlefield. 

Strengths

A host of different lists to choose from

The Middle-earth Strategy Battle Game is broken down into Army Lists. Each one represents a faction with their own special rules from a certain point in Middle-earth’s history. Rohan has 10 Army Lists to choose from, such as Riders of Théoden, Army of Edoras, or the Fords of Isen, but Rohan models can also be taken in four other lists with other factions, such as Men of the West and The Grief of Éomer. Having the choice of 14 lists means you can have a Rohan force ready for any Scenario.

A wide and varied choice of Heroes

Rohan has some of the most famous and recognisable Heroes from The Lord of the RingsTM movies and novels, with the likes of Théoden, Éomer, Éowyn, Helm Hammerhand, and Héra. With each Hero adding something different to your army, you can adapt your force to counter any foe.

Excellent Cavalry

It goes without saying that Rohan are the horse lords – they even have a special rule with that very name, amongst a few others. Riders of Rohan can gallop effortlessly over the battlefield with their 10" move, getting into the perfect position to strike on their terms. Due to the Cavalry Charge rule and the bonuses it provides, when the forces of Rohan choose to engage, they can sweep their foes from the field.

Bows

Every Rider of Rohan comes with a bow. Every single one. Riders of Rohan can unleash deadly volleys of arrows to thin out their opponent’s ranks before lining up a glorious cavalry charge to win the day. A common tactic for Rohan players is to ‘kite and shoot’ their opponent until the time is right – at first light on the fifth day.

Weaknesses

Low model count when using only Cavalry

Taking an all-Cavalry list can quickly erode the points you have to spend on your army. After taking your favourite Heroes, you may not have a lot of space for a suitable model count. Experienced Rohan players will try to find that perfect balance between having all the cool stuff and including enough models. The last thing you want is to Charge in and then quickly be mobbed by hordes of Orcs!

Fortunately, Heroes like Éomer and Helm Hammerhand can easily make up for their army’s lower model count, each capable of carving a swathe through their foes.

Low Defence

Riders and Warriors of Rohan don’t tend to wear a lot of heavy armour, relying instead on keeping the foe at a distance until the time is right. As the majority of the army has a humble Defence 5, Rohan armies can’t take as many hits as others, or risk being exposed to enemy shooting for too long. Use the speed of your Cavalry to close in quickly with the foe, or ensure that there is plenty of intervening terrain between your warriors and enemy missile weapons.

Getting bogged down

Rohan armies, especially all-Cavalry armies, will often find themselves outnumbered on the battlefield. With Rohan’s strength being in the cavalry charge, losing Priority roll-offs and getting counter-charged by hordes of infantry can spell doom for a force of Rohirrim. Holding some of your Cavalry back in a flying reserve will give you a second wave of charging riders that can help toImitigate losing a key Priority roll-off.

Too much choice

Whilst this is a nicer problem to have, Rohan players have lots of awesome Heroes to choose from. In total, Rohan has 21 Hero profiles from both the Armies of the Lord of the RingsTM and the Armies of Middle-earthTM supplements. Mustering a Rohan army will leave you spoilt for choice! But I’ll give you some advice… Éomer, choose Éomer!** You’re then allowed to shout “To the King!” every time you move him.

Strategy

Using Cavalry

As we now know, if you choose to muster a Rohan force centred around Cavalry, you will often find yourself outnumbered, but there are tactics to help you achieve victory even against the vast legions of the enemy.

When starting the game, you ideally want to identify areas on the board you can use to effectively ‘kite and shoot’ your opponent with your bows. For the first few turns of the game, you want to try to bring your opponent’s model count down, and if possible, draw them into a better position for when you eventually Charge – for example, encircling them or leading them away from vital objectives that your fast-moving Cavalry can easily return to as the battle progresses.

Models armed with bows can move up to half their Move Value and still Shoot. This means that your Riders of Rohan can Move up to 5" (almost the full Move of an average Infantry model) and still loose their arrows. When this tactic is used correctly, your Riders will always just be out of reach – but can always forgo a turn of Shooting in order to leave the enemy behind if they need to. This is a strong tactic as it gives your opponent one of two choices: run at you and risk breaking up their formation, or stand still whilst being pelted by arrows. 

Choosing the right list for your playstyle

As noted above, Rohan players have a wide choice of Army Lists to muster from. Each one of these lists has different special rules to represent a particular scene from the films or books. Some lists are Cavalry-heavy, whereas others are mainly made up of Warriors of Rohan, such as Defenders of Helm’s Deep. When choosing and subsequently playing a certain list, you want to make sure you maximise these special rules to your advantage.

For example, if your playstyle is to lean into the ‘kite and shoot’ mechanic of the army, you wouldn’t choose the list ‘Ride Out’, as it features a special rule called Now for wrath, now for ruin, and the red dawn, which means that all your Cavalry models must Charge if able. On the flip side, if you want an army that crushes the foe as it sallies forth, then Ride Out may be for you, as that same special rule makes your Cavalry even better on the Charge!

If you’re looking to field more Infantry than Cavalry, then I recommend Defenders of the Hornburg, as this list has Héra, the Bride of Death and the furious Helm, Wraith of the Hornburg leading Warriors of Rohan. I’ve played this list a lot over the past year, and have found Helm to be one of the most enjoyable Heroes in the game as he goes around punching foes with his bare ‘hammerhands’.

Finally, if you’re looking for a more balanced Rohan Army, Riders of Théoden and Riders of Éomer will be right up your street. The Riders of Théoden Army has a special rule to represent the greatest cavalry charge in cinematic history, while the Riders of Éomer can bring Gandalf the White to battle, who can utilise the light of the dawn to blind your enemy as you close with them

Heroes

The biggest challenge you will have is choosing which of your favourite characters to take. However in certain lists, some Heroes are crucial.

In the Riders of Éomer list, the Marshal of the Riddermark becomes unleashed. He gains the special rule “To the King”, allowing him to call a free Heroic Combat once per turn. A Heroic Combat allows you to Move and Fight again if you slay all the models you began the phase in Combat with. Combining this with the Cavalry Charge bonuses turns Éomer into a meatgrinder who can happily slay four or five enemies a turn. His horse, Firefoot, also has a whopping 12" Move, just to make sure no one escapes his wrath.

Another unique Hero is Lief, Page of Helm. Lief is not a melee beast like Éomer. He will often find himself sitting behind the battle lines handing out the Orders from Edoras, buffing your Army when needed. Lief can issue up to five orders per game and each order, when used at the right time, can spell doom for your opponent. For example, he can make all Rohan Hero models within 3" declare a Heroic Combat for free, which can be devastating. He can also allow your models to Move further or Shoot more accurately. All of this makes him a great, versatile and cost-effective Hero option.

Finally, we have the humble Captain of Rohan. As Rohan has so many named Heroes to choose from, Captains are often overlooked, but they can be great additions to your army.

There are two main reasons for this. The first is their points cost – as a cheap option they allow you to fit more models in your army compared to taking an expensive named Hero. Secondly, every Captain is able to call a Heroic March. When they do this, they can make Infantry models move an additional 3" and Cavalry move an additional 5". The only caveat is that you are not allowed to Charge if you take part in a Heroic March. Nevertheless, if you want to get into a better position quicker, or beat your opponent to an objective, Heroic March speeds you on your way.

Final Thoughts

The Kingdom of Rohan is a fantastic faction for both veterans and beginners alike. They have access to so many different Army Lists and Heroes that once you have an army fully mustered, you’ll be able to try out different rules, tactics and playstyles for ages to come. Before long you will be fearing no darkness and shouting “Forth Eorlingas!”.

* Yes, Kalman has tried to squeeze in as many lines from the films as he possibly can.
** We think the Third Marshal of the Riddermark might be Kalman’s favourite.

We’re a few months into the season of Warhammer Age of Sigmar, so it’s time for the first of the quarterly Battlescroll updates. 

Points adjustments are complemented by some important rules changes to improve balance in the Mortal Realms and below you can find a summary of the most significant updates.

Universal

There are a couple of changes that open up list building options. Firstly, a number of infantry heroes can now be included in regiments, and a lot of units have had their reinforcement restrictions lifted. 

Grand Alliance Order

A couple of rules from the Scourge of Aqshy season rules have proven to be more powerful than anticipated and so are being toned down a little. Fyreslayers can no longer use Blazing Impetus to move after being set up, and for the Idoneth Deepkin, Abyssal Dweller no longer reduces enemy movement. The War Hydra from the Cities of Sigmar battletome supplement has also had its Impossible to Destroy ability tweaked as it was proving, well, impossible to destroy.

Grand Alliance Chaos

On the Skaven side, Krittok Foulblade can now use his A Reputation for Cunning ability without needing to spend a Command Point, and the Lightning Master ability of the Warlock Galvaneer is now guaranteed to activate, yes-yes! For the Slaves to Darkness the Oracular Visions of the Sorcerer Lord are now more reliable, but units with an Ensorcelled Banner can no longer switch Pledge to Chaos keywords. You chose your Dark God and now you’re stuck with them!

The newest addition to Grand Alliance Chaos – the Helsmiths of Hashut – have had their battle formations updated. The studio felt they were not having the impact hoped for and so the Zharrdron now have some new tools as they seek to claim dominion over the Mortal Realms.

Grand Alliance Death

The Nighthaunt have had the most changes in this quarter’s update with improvements to the Lord Vitriolic and Scriptor Mortis, while the Shadowy Aura heroic trait now blocks visibility to Nighthaunt infantry and cavalry, and there’s been a boost to the Death Stalkers battle formation. The Ossiarch Bonereapers no longer have to pay the Relentless Discipline ‘tax’ for reinforced units, so abilities such as Pitiless Assault just got cheaper for your larger units.

The Scourge of Aqshy Vengorian Lord has been proving slightly too powerful so the Soulblight Gravelords Monster Frenzied Surge ability has been adjusted.

Grand Alliance Destruction

Finally, the Gatebreaker Mega-Gargant from the Scourge of Aqshy has undergone a little change so that he doesn’t form an over-the-top combo with the new Rock-hurlers.

The ironclad gates have opened, and the Khazalite Holds are on the warpath. Meet the new Warhammer Age of Sigmar faction!

The Khazalites consider themselves the truest and most respectable of all duardin, as it is they who venerate the Ancestor Gods with due reverence, and they who maintain the honourable traditions of their forebears. It is not with mercantile pragmatism or mercenary fury that the realms will be cleansed of the hated Skaven, but with stony resilience and relentless determination.

The Khazalite Holds are preparing to march on the Mortal Realms with a new Army Set – packed with miniatures and a battletome – and followed by a range of other new kits.

Led by the mighty Hjulda Drakkblud, this force of indomitable warriors has everything the Khazalites do best: tough armour, deadly hammers, and a cannon big enough to blow a hole through a Mega-Gargant. It’s a complete Spearhead army in a box, and also serves as the perfect starting point for a wider Khazalite Holds collection.

Hjulda herself is legendary among those Khazalites who have rejoined the surface world, as she and her Clanguard search endlessly for lost karaks that might yet be reclaimed, hopeful that the next might finally be the home of her lost clan.

Accompanying her are 10 Clanshields – doughty warriors armed with a variety of Kromdron weapons – which can be axes, hammers, or a mix – that specialise in taking out enemy infantry. Clad in stout armour, they are difficult to shift, and they invoke the names and deeds of their ancestors to bring them strength in battle.

Of particular note are the massive Gholems of Gazul – animated stone constructs that honour the Ancestor God of the underworlds. They stand sentinel inside duardin tombs until called upon by a mournful dirge of remembrance, silently trudging into battle with stoic purpose as they send scores of foes to the Realm of Death with great swings of their stone hammers.

Supplying the duardin with long-ranged firepower is the Oathkeeper Cannon. Combining engineering excellence with esoteric runecraft, these war machines tear through enemy ranks with ease. As the firing rune is struck, it’s almost as if Grungni himself has smashed the foes of the duardin with his mighty forging hammer.

The army set also includes the new battletome, packed with background lore on this new faction and the rules you need to unleash them in battle. It has a special cover, which you’ll only find in the army set, and there are also 53 warscroll cards.

Battletome: Khazalite Holds

The battletome will also be coming out separately at a later date, packed with the same in-depth lore and inspiring artwork. It’s not just the newcomers who occupy the battletome’s pages either, as the Fyreslayers will be joining their duardin cousins (more on them lower down this article!).

Beyond the Army Set, a second wave of Khazalite Holds units expand the army even further, starting with the Thrynns and Runewrights that lead them.

Thrynn and Runewright

Thrynns are the lords of the Karaks, chosen by their fellow nobles. Armed and armoured with the finest runic artefacts, they lead the war throngs into battle. Runewrights are masters of arcane forging, able to utilise the resonant magic of the runes.

High Kyng Valankrom

Above them all stands High Kyng Valankrom, the supreme leader of the Khazalite Holds, crowned by Grungni himself. He is a ferocious warrior and shrewd statesman, unquestioned in his authority, and he rides into battle on an immense stone construct known as a War Throne. The War Throne moves across the earth, impelled by powerful duardin magic.

This jaw-dropping centrepiece kit also builds a Thrynn on War Throne. It is a great honour to ride such a war altar into battle, and it inspires nearby Khazalite Holds troops to ever greater feats.

Clangunners

The Clanshields from the army set aren’t the only new infantry – they’re joined by the Clangunners. Picking off enemies at range with accurate thrundok rifles or devastating them closer up with thrundrin shotcannons, they excel in both defence and attack.

Stonebreaker Mortar

The Oathkeeper Cannon from the army box can alternatively be built as a Stonebreaker Mortar. This devastating war machine specialises in destroying enemy infantry and, when the correct rune is struck, can even devastate more than one target with its blast.

Valayan Guardians

Among the finest troops available to a Khazalite Hold, Valayan Guardians fight for the very heart of duardin society and place the defence of their kin as the highest honour. Valaya is the ancestor of hearth and home – known as the defender – and the Guardians believe that she watches over their every battle, which inspires them to fight with incredible tenacity and resilience (even for a duardin!)

Gholems of Valaya

Speaking of Valaya, the Gholems of Gazul also have an alternate build option, making them Gholems of Valaya instead. Carved into the image of the warrior goddess, they are treated with utmost reverence by her followers.

Fyreslayers

As mentioned above, the Fyreslayers – or Grimmdron – have become part of the Khazalite Holds. After decades of slow attrition grinding down their magmaholds, and a disastrous attack on their spiritual capital by a tenuous alliance of Helsmiths and Skaven, the slayers of Grimnir are filled with a burning need for vengeance.

This means that you’ll be able to use your existing miniatures with the new battletome, whether you want to run a full Fyreslayers army, or want to include some alongside the new Kromdron. We’ll be talking more about how this affects them as we get closer to release.

Ormyr and Ashtongue

The Fyreslayers are getting a new wandering beastmaster, Ormyr, for their war party, who comes accompanied by his kyndledroth Ashtongue. This eclectic pair are known across the realms of the Khazalites, notorious for turning up out of nowhere to offer their aid on the eve of battle.

Regiment of Renown

Troubled by the fall of the Fyreslayer kingdom, Fjori and his like-minded Grimmdron sell their services to the highest bidder – as long as they can also slake their desire for vengeance. This new Regiment of Renown can be used by any Order army, and includes an Auric Flamekeeper, a Grimhold Exile, and five Hearthguard Berzerkers.

Spearhead: Magmic Fyrd

Burning with vengeance for the destruction of their former holds and lands, the Magmic Fyrds of the Grimmdron seek out foes wherever they can find them. This Fyreslayer-themed Spearhead features a monstrous Magmadroth ridden by a Runefather, a Runesmiter, nine Vulkyn Flameseekers, and five Auric Hearthguard.

That’s a lot to see from a brand new faction, isn’t it? We’ll have loads more details for you as we get closer to pre-order day, so stick with us if you want to know more about the Khazalite Holds.

The Legion of the Damned step forth from a halo of witchfire to unleash burning retribution on the xenos brutes. With fire and fury, they take on the elite Ork Nobz Mob and bring aid to the beleaguered planet. 

Each spectral Legionnaire is covered in skeletal details and wreathed in ethereal flames. Their true nature eludes even the most persistent of Inquisitors, and though they can be credited with turning the tide of countless battles, few know to whom – or what – they owe their lives.

The Legion’s mysterious, ghostly nature makes this kill team play wildly differently from other Space Marines, as they must solidify their connection to the material plane over time to reach the height of their power. Early in the game, they move and fight slower than regular Space Marines, but as turning points tick over and their form solidifies, they grow to become terrifying, spectral monsters, bursting at the seams with eldritch fire.

Against them stands a team of vicious Boss Nobz – the cream of the Orks’ elite warriors. You may have seen them in our reveal, or inside Codex: Orks, but the Kill Team:Armageddon boxed set is where they will be available first.

These hardcore veterans have survived wars on dozens of worlds and tower over their lesser kin, adorned in thick armour plates and carrying a wide variety of eclectic Ork weapons. Some are obsessed with dakka and dual-wield kustom shootas, while others delight in flame-fuelled destruction and heft an enormous skorcha* into the killzone.

Speaking of killzones, a whole new set of terrain is the battleground for this clash of fire and fury, with wrecked vehicles and crumbling buildings painting a picture of the devastation unleashed upon Armageddon.

The Killzone: Armageddon terrain is designed to stylistically fit in with the existing Battlezone Fronteris kits, but in a more battle-worn state. You get two sturdy bunkers, which have their own rules for the desperate close-quarters fights that happen when an unlucky operative has to storm one. There are also ruins and scatter terrain, including a wrecked Redemptor Dreadnought and Rogal Dorn Battle Tank.

To top it all off, you get the customary sets of datacards to help keep your important rules in mind, and the Kill Team: Armageddon Dossier, which contains all of the rules you need for both kill teams as well as background lore on the Legion of the Damned, Ork Nobz, and the desperate times that threw these bitter foes together.

We can’t wait to see the Legion of the Damned back on the tabletop, and we’ll be taking a closer look at their rules (for both Kill Team AND Warhammer 40,000) as we get closer to release. While we wait for them to rematerialise, check out the other big reveals from the Big Autumn Preview.

Dire times have drawn the vaunted Adeptus Custodes into the fight, and now their elite Aquilon Terminators deploy alongside the next new Codex for Warhammer 40,000.

The warriors chosen to wear advanced suits of Aquilon Terminator armour are the true cream of the crop, who enter battle clad in some of the rarest and most durable plate the Imperium has ever seen. These ancient relics are usually outfitted for combat with one of two loadouts – either with lastrum storm bolters and swift Solarite power talons, or adrathic combi-destructors and devastating Solarite power gauntlets.

Like Allarus Terminators, these veteran warriors are immensely durable and can wipe out units many times their size. Their miniatures are accordingly covered in fine ornamental details, making each Terminator a display-worthy piece that together look awesome arrayed together on the battlefield.

The new Aquilon Terminators can be used in both the Age of Darkness and the 41st Millennium. Their Warhammer: The Horus Heresy rules can be found in the Liber Custodes: The Forces of the Emperor Army Book while their Warhammer 40,000 rules will be in the new Codex: Adeptus Custodes. This book follows the pattern of the previous Orks and Space Marines Codexes, with the standard softback release packing tons of background lore, hobby guides, and army rules together in a decorative slipcase.

This Codex also marks an epochal change for the Adeptus Custodes as a faction, as their datasheets are fundamentally rescaled to reflect the near-mythical demigod heroes we know and love from the lore. Even the most ‘basic’ Custodian fights at a power level beyond most Space Marine heroes, with points levels and squad sizes adjusted to make them the true most elite army in the game.*

The new Codex will be accompanied by a Combat Patrol – the perfect place to enter this new era of Imperial domination, packed with powerful warriors and advanced technology.

A Shield Captain leads a potent strike force of six Sentinel Guard and three Venatari, backed up by a towering Contemptor-Achillus Dreadnought. If you’re not worried about using this box in games of Combat Patrol, you can also build the three squads in alternate configurations, making this one of the most flexible boxes around.

Like other new Codexes in the 11th edition, you’ll also be able to pick up a faction Command Pack containing reference cards and useful tokens – invaluable for keeping your attention on the game while bolt rounds and blades fly.

This new Codex coincides with a range of newer Custodian kits getting their standalone releases, which can all be used in both Warhammer 40,000 AND Warhammer: The Horus Heresy.

The following kits are getting swanky new packaging bearing the logos for both game systems:

  • Shield Captain

  • Custodian Guard Sodality

  • Sentinel Guard Sodality

  • Venatari Sodality

  • Custodian Dreadnought

  • Telemon Heavy Dreadnought

  • Gyrfalcon Jetbike Sodality

  • Pallas Grav-attack 

  • Caladius Grav-tank

  • Coronus Grav-carrier

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.title: The Big Autumn Preview – Roleplay in the underhive
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: New Necromunda game revealed!
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
Warhammer Necromunda Roleplay offers completely different ways to explore the underhive, and you’ll soon learn that it’s a large and dangerous place with much more to see and be killed by than just gang battles.

Been wondering why the new Necromunda Core Set proudly displays the word “Skirmish” on the front of the box? Well, it’s to distinguish it from the new Necromunda Roleplay. As the name suggests, it’s a fully-fledged, miniatures-driven RPG, allowing you to participate in immersive stories that will take you from the underhive to the ash wastes. 

You play as a group of bounty-hunting Venators taking on jobs set by the Arbitrator, the equivalent of a games master, who presents the story to the other players, adjudicating on the rules of the game, and unfolding the narrative created by the actions of the players. It’s compatible with the full range of Necromunda miniatures, and comes with some fantastic and characterful new models, starting with those representing your team – these four Iconic Characters.

These player characters are an Escher Assassin, Orlock Gunslinger, Squat Fixer, and Goliath Champion. They each have rules in the box to get you started quickly, and they all have alternate builds if you want to craft your own Venators.

You’ll encounter a variety of interesting personalities in your journeys, and some of those in the two included adventures can be nicely represented by the five Adversary miniatures in the box – a Scabber, a Saboteur, a Hive Preacher, a Cadaver Merchant, and a Heretek with a servo-skull.*

Of course, no expedition through the underhive or ash wastes is complete without gunning down some goons – step forward Hive Scum. These eight no-name mooks can be built with a wide variety of weapon options and give you plenty of opportunity to test your skills in marksmanship and swordplay as you hunt down targets and investigate mysterious goings-on.

Along with the 18 brand-new plastic miniatures, the Core Set includes the 224-page Core Rulebook, which includes plenty of lore, along with rules for playing the game, creating your own characters and how they advance and improve their skills between adventures. There are also tips for the Arbitrator and two complete adventures – ‘An Abominable Intelligence’ where you hunt down a Van Saar Heretek, and ‘The Pilgrimage of Bones’, which sees you tasked with taking out a Cawdor preacher on behalf of the Corpse Harvesters Guild.

At some point in your adventures, you’re going to get into a fight, and the box includes two double-sided card playmats depicting regions of the underhive and ash wastes where your Venators will face their foes, and 11 player handouts for quick rules reference for the miniatures in the box. There’s also an Arbitrator’s screen packed with useful reference information for the Arbitrator, and allowing them to hide their devious plans from the players.

Combat encounters play out with a system that will be recognisable to Necromunda Skirmish players, utilising miniatures who have Single and Double actions, rolls to hit and injuries – all with a roleplay twist. You’ll also notice a D10 and D100 in the box, alongside the familiar D6, Firepower and Injury dice, which work with your characters’ skills to show you what you need to roll.

In essence, whenever you want to do something, whether it’s trying to fill a Hive Scum with las-rounds or intimidate a source into giving up information, you need to roll below a target score based on your skill value and a difficulty modifier. Let’s take a look at a character sheet to see some of these.

Ophelia Skar here has a WS of 61 and BS of 49, so she’s more proficient with her stiletto sword than her laspistol. She has a variety of skills, including Acrobatics, Intimidate and Stealth, which will inform how you play her in your adventures. The other Iconic Characters have different mixes of skills and abilities, so working together is key to overcoming foes and whatever cunning obstacles your Arbitrator lays for you.

If you want to make your own characters, there are 50 blank character sheets in the box, and the Core Rulebook contains full rules for creating Venators hailing from the six Clan Houses, each with their own backgrounds, archetypes, and skill sets. There is also a seventh origin, the Underhiver, with their own selection of backgrounds and archetypes, as well as the option to play a Squat. 

Necromunda Roleplay will launch alongside the first in a series of expansions – Journal Apocrypha: Denizens of the Hive – Adversaries Book 1. This 48-page journal includes profiles for 51 additional potential Adversaries – or allies – using the wide variety of Necromunda miniatures.** 

These range from members of the six Clan Houses to Enforcers, Ogryns, hive dwellers, exotic beasts, and even the infamous Kal Jericho and Scabs, who’ve been known to recruit Venators to aid them on their own adventures. If your Arbitrator is feeling particularly mean, you might even end up facing off against a mighty Ambot…

Both the Warhammer Necromunda Roleplay Core Set and the first journal will be available soon, and we’ll delve deeper into the game and how it works before release. In the meantime, head back to the Big Autumn Preview Hub to see what else we’ve revealed.

https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.description: A new team bounces onto the Blood Bowl pitch.
https://www.warhammer-community.com/en-g.content_html:
From deep underground come the Night Goblins team for Blood Bowl, and they’ve brought Squigs with them. Lots of Squigs!

Night Goblins are known for cackling maniacally, being obsessed with mushrooms, and using moon iconography. You could say they’re a few toadstools short of a cluster, but when it comes to Blood Bowl that can be a blessing.

While their overground cousins rely on secret weapons, and other underground teams use technology or fleshcraft to win games, the Night Goblins have their vicious, bouncy friends, introducing four new positionals – Cave Squigs, Squig Wranglers, Squig Hoppers, and Squig Herders. The kit includes two of each of these, along with six Night Goblin Linemen.

Goblin Linemen might not run rampant on the pitch but they are annoying little critters who are difficult to get hold of with Dodge and Stunty, and also difficult to get away from with Taunt and Shadowing. Cave Squigs and Squig Hoppers both have Pogo, making them pretty mobile, but you’ll need to keep your Squig Herders nearby so they don’t succumb to the ominously-named Squig Rage. Finally, the Squig Wranglers are ST7 Ball & Chain players – what could possibly go wrong?

The Night Goblins are a fun, characterful team that bring a lot of new options to the Blood Bowl pitch. As with any Stunty team, they’ll need a skilful (and lucky) coach to get the best out of them, but if you can control the chaos, you’ll be onto a winner.

Rules for unleashing all this Squiggy goodness can be found in the forthcoming 23rd issue of Spike! Journal.

It’s also packed with background on Night Goblin teams, including the legendary Eight Peaks Loonatics, rules for the spiteful shroom and bat Squig balls that come with the team kit, a coaches’ guide to get the best from your gobbos, and all your favourite regular columns such as Ask Lord Borak and Coffin Corner.
